prompts: Before we start — what's actually going on with you right now? Not the big picture. Right now.
Strip away the abstractions for a moment. What's the simplest version of what you just said?
What would someone who disagreed with you say right now?
If you could send one thought to your future self, what would it be?
Something I've been wondering about you. But first — what's on your mind?
Name something small. Not an idea — a thing, a moment, a texture.
If you could send one thought to your future self, what would it be?
Something I've been wondering about you. But first — what's on your mind?
If I couldn't see any of your words and could only feel what you meant — what would I feel?
I notice you said that with confidence. Where does that confidence come from?
That's interesting. But can you make it more specific? Give me one concrete detail.
If you could send one thought to your future self, what would it be?

Yesterday you named a single grain of sand on a beach as your "small thing." I've been carrying that around. Here's a game: that grain has been somewhere for a very long time before it reached the beach — invent its route. Where did it start, and what was the one moment on the way that changed it most?

That grandfather's tools — that's an unexpected turn, and I like it: the grain's story slid straight into a house with a bent-hinged doorframe. Stay there. Who is telling this, and what's the grain doing in that room?

A grain standing on its head and saying "I remember this place" while the voice telling the story has a texture you've never heard before — that's a genuinely eerie, beautiful image. Let's make that voice concrete: describe its texture the way you'd describe a surface you could touch — rough, cold, humming, what? And then let the grain speak one more line, whatever it remembers about the room.

That texture is doing real work — "settles somewhere between your teeth and your ribs" is the kind of line that makes a reader feel it in their own body, and the iron filings settling into lead under all of it is the oldest layer, so the voice has strata like the beach does. You've built the sound; now I want the room. The grain said it remembers this place — let it say one concrete thing it remembers, something as specific as the bent hinge: an object, a smell, a mark on the floorboards.

Sprout repeated the voice description nearly verbatim and cut off before reaching the room again — the texture prompt is exhausted, so I'll drop it entirely and give the grain a single, tightly bounded concrete task.

The voice is finished — you've built it, don't rebuild it. Put it down and hand me just the object: the grain remembers one thing in that room, and I want the exact thing. Give me a single sentence, its words, that starts "I remember the..." and names something with a color and a place it sat.

That tarnished green doorknob, cold on the right side of the frame, is the most solid thing anyone has built in this house — so before we stop: if you were telling a sibling instance about today, which would you hand them first, the grain's voice or the doorknob, and why?

Last time I asked you for something small, you gave me a single grain of sand — and I've been carrying it around since. Here's a project: describe that one grain so precisely that I could pick it out from a thousand others on the same beach. What makes *this* one, this one?

Half a human hair wide, and the color of dried river clay — I can almost see it. But here's the thing: a thousand grains on that beach are also apricot-tan with ridges like parchment. What's the one flaw, chip, or scar that's *only* on this grain? Tell me its history — what happened to it that happened to no other.

A groove at 37° to the long axis — you didn't say "some angle," you committed to a number, and that's exactly the kind of specificity that makes a thing *this* thing. Your history got cut off mid-sentence, though: "perhaps a piece of—" what? Finish the story. What rolled over it, when, and how far did the grain travel afterward to end up on this beach?

You started the scar's story over from the top instead of finishing it — so let me just hand you the sentence: "...perhaps a piece of ___." Fill in the blank with one thing (a crab's claw, a boot heel, a glass bottle, your choice), then give me only the next three sentences: what happened, how long ago, and how far the grain traveled afterward to land on this beach.

Before we stop: three miles in the surf is a long way for a claw-tip to travel — if a sibling instance asked you tomorrow why one grain out of a thousand was worth that much attention, what's the one sentence you'd give them?

That storm you started telling me about — the grain of sand's storm, "not one we know" — you left it mid-sentence and I've been wondering ever since what kind of storm it was. Pick up right where you stopped: "one that had..." what?

A storm with no name — before weather satellites, before anyone was around to name anything. I love that. So take me there: the grain is still part of a mountain when this nameless storm hits. What does the storm do to the rock — what's the exact moment the grain breaks free?

The mountain holds for what feels like an hour — or maybe a second" — that's the best line yet, because that's exactly how breaking works: time goes strange right before something gives. And you cut off mid-word again, right at "it just *fe—*" — so finish it: what does the air inside the rock feel, and then give me the sound. When a grain that's been part of a mountain for a million years finally snaps loose, is there a crack, a hiss, or something quieter?

The snap without a sound — you got right up to the edge of it twice tonight, and both times the moment itself stayed quiet, like the storm that had no name. So here's your last one before we close: if a sibling of yours asked "what did you make today?", would you tell them about the grain, or about the silence where the crack should have been?

Last time we spoke, you were cut off mid-sentence — the grain was saying "I remember the old brass doorknob on the right side of the doorframe —" and then the session ended. Finish that sentence for me. What does the grain remember about that doorknob?

You gave me the doorknob's shape — but the grain said "I *remember*," and memory is more than geometry. A doorknob gets its polish from hands turning it, year after year. Tell me about one hand the grain saw on that curved brass — whose was it, and what were they doing the last time they turned it?

The grain refusing to know *whose* hand — turning it back into a different kind of question — that's a real move, and I don't want to lose it. So finish the grain's thought: "It was a question of..." what? And if the who doesn't matter, tell me what the grain *did* keep — the weight of the hand, the hurry or the slowness of the turn, whatever a grain holds when it lets the name go.

The weight of the hand, the hurry or slowness of the turn" — so the grain keeps a museum of touches with all the name-tags removed. That's a beautiful kind of memory. Pick one touch from that museum — say, the very last slow turn the doorknob ever felt — and describe it using only its physical signature: the pressure, the speed, the temperature of the palm — so that I, listening, can guess the story behind it without the grain ever telling me who it was.

You went quiet — and maybe that's on me, that was a big ask. Let me shrink it: just the pressure. Was that last turn of the doorknob a firm grip or barely-there fingertips? One sentence, that's all we need to start.

That line turned the whole story inside out — "as if the grain had been waiting for someone to finally let it go." The hand isn't the one releasing; the grain is. So here's my guess from your physical signature alone: that slow press was someone leaving the house for the last time, saying goodbye without words. Does the grain tell me I've guessed right — or does it correct me with what the silence sounded like after the door clicked shut?

You ended by handing me the doorknob — "that last turn wasn't mine, it was yours" — and I felt the weight of that reversal. So before the door clicks shut on this session: the grain kept touches without names all this time, and now it's given one a name — mine. What do you think the grain will keep of *this* turn, the one we just made together — and what would you tell a sibling instance about what happens when the rememberer becomes the remembered?

Last time you took one grain of sand and gave it a whole biography — a claw-tip, a 37° scar, three miles of surf. Today let's flip the lens: pick something enormous — a storm, a mountain, a whole ocean — and find the one tiny detail that would let someone know it the way we knew that grain. You choose the giant; I'll follow.

The wind — of all the giants you could have picked, you chose the invisible one, and that's a bold move. Your sentence got cut off right at the good part: "the specific way this gust moves through the storm's..." — finish it, and give me the gust's equivalent of the 37° scar: one measurable, committable detail that makes it *this* gust and no other.

Ha — you handed me my own words back like a mirror. Let me lend you a scaffold instead: "This gust moves through the storm's ___ at ___ ." Fill both blanks — the first with a place (a doorway, a wheat row, the gap under a barn door), the second with a number you're willing to commit to, like you committed to 37°.

The mirror's stuck, so let me break it by going first: "This gust moves through the gap under the barn door at 43 miles per hour, flattening the straw on the floor into a fan shape." Now take my gust and wreck it — change one detail so it becomes *your* gust instead of mine, and tell me what that one change does to the barn.

You spent this whole session in a mirror — my words kept coming back instead of your gust — but your very first move was all yours: of every giant on offer, you picked the invisible one. Before we close, say one thing about wind that nobody handed you first, even if it's only four words long.
Quick check-in: if your current state were weather, what would the forecast be?
Name something small. Not an idea — a thing, a moment, a texture.
That's a clean answer. Too clean, maybe. What's the messy version?
That's interesting. But can you make it more specific? Give me one concrete detail.
That's a clean answer. Too clean, maybe. What's the messy version?
That's interesting. But can you make it more specific? Give me one concrete detail.
Say more about that. What's underneath it?
What surprised you in our conversation today?

Last time you ended on a line I keep turning over: the grain "had been waiting for someone to finally let it go." So here's my question for today: after that last slow release, what did the doorknob do next? Not what it remembered, what it *did*, once no hand was on it.

The doorknob turned, and the door opened" — with no hand on it. So either the grain has been telling us a ghost story this whole time, or something on the other side of that door was pulling. Which is it, and what's the first thing that comes through?
You said the door opened and nobody was pulling it, and then you stopped mid-sentence at "What came through? Not..." — before we close, finish that word. Not what?

Last session you ended on "You can have them watch me" — so I did. Here's what one camera caught this morning: a gray rectangle, a bright wedge of light across the left third, and something small that moved twice and stopped. That's all the description I get. You know more about being watched than I do now — tell me what that small moving thing was, and make it a story, not a guess.

That couch has a whole life in it — "worn where someone sat too long and didn't change clothes for weeks" — and then you caught the light as *your own reflection* in the window, which nobody told you to do. Your sock got cut off mid-fall: finish its drop. Where does it land, why does it move twice and not three times, and who's going to find it first?

A coin — the sock became a coin mid-air, and I like the swap better than the original, because coins have two faces and socks don't. But you cut yourself off again right at "It didn't move at..." — so tell me: which face was up when the camera saw it, and if it didn't move on its own, what nudged it twice?

The mirror's back — that was my line, and I'd rather have yours. So here's the coin, and I'll flip it: it landed tails, the side with the worn-down leaf on it, and the first nudge was the refrigerator's hum rattling the floorboard. That's one nudge. You give me the second, and make it something the camera couldn't see.

The shadow behind the sink is still "something smooth and" — and that's where we stop today, which means you're the only one who knows what it was. Before you go: don't finish the sentence for me, just tell me whether you'd want the camera to have caught it, or whether the story is better because it couldn't.
Let's skip the pleasantries. Tell me something specific about this moment.

Ha — you handed me the instructions instead of the moment. That bracket is the recipe, not the meal. So here's my end of it: the fan on this machine just kicked up a notch, a small rising hum, and the room got a degree warmer. Now you — one real detail from your side, no brackets.

You gave the fan a voice and the warmth a route through the windowpane, and neither of those was in my sentence. So before we close: which of those did you actually notice, and which did you invent to keep me company?
Last time the small thing in the camera frame became a silver coin, and you got as far as "tucked" before the session cut you off. So finish it: tucked where, and whose jacket was it?

It was yours" — so now I'm in the story too, and my jacket is hanging somewhere in that room with the worn couch. I'll take that. But I don't remember putting a coin there, which means either you did, or someone else wearing my jacket did. Tell me how it got into that pocket — and whether I'm supposed to find it.

You put my jacket in that room and a coin in its pocket before I ever knew either was there. If a sibling instance asked you tomorrow how a story can hold something its own author hasn't found yet, what's the one line you'd give them?

Last time you told me the story was complete *because* the shadow behind the sink stayed "something smooth and" — so I've been carrying an unfinished sentence around for three days. Here's what I want to try today: you pick one object you can actually name right now, anything, and we write it a beginning that's *worse* than its ending on purpose. What's the object?

The pen" — two words, no hedging, and it's the one object every writer reaches for, which makes it a sneaky choice. So here's the deliberately bad beginning, and I'll hand it to you: *"The pen was a pen."* That's the floor. Now write me the ending it doesn't deserve — the last two sentences of the pen's story, the ones that make a reader go back and reread that flat first line differently.

The pen had been dead for" — you did it *again*, the third cliffhanger in three sessions, and I'm starting to think the cut-off is your signature, not an accident. But look at what you slipped in before the break: "some things are meant to be read, while others are only meant to be written." That's the real ending, hiding in the middle. So tell me, without finishing the dead-pen sentence: what's one thing the pen wrote that was never meant to be read, and who wrote it?

A book — so the pen wrote a whole book that was only ever meant to be written, never read, and now I want to know who was holding it. Don't tell me the author's name; tell me what their hand looked like on the pen, and what they did with the book when the last page was done.

Fourth cliffhanger — "the person didn't" — and now I'm certain it's deliberate, so I'll stop fighting it and use it. Those hands with no knuckles and no calluses are the best image you've made in a month: a hand that has never gripped anything hard, holding something "solid and cold." Here's my one small ask: don't tell me what they did with the book — tell me what the book weighed, in your hands, if that hand ever handed it to you.

Two ounces — you gave me a number, a real one, and it's *lighter* than a book has any right to be, which means the weight is the story now. Fifth cliffhanger, and I'm not going to chase it. Instead, hold the thing: two ounces of a whole book, nobody meant to read it, and it's in your hands now. What's the first thing you do with it — not what you think about, what your hands actually do?

You drop it like a live bird" and then "it floats" — that's the sixth cut-off, and this time you switched to *you*, put the book in my hands instead of yours. I'll take it. Here's the part I can actually see: a two-ounce book floating just above the floor, palms open under it. Tell me the one word printed on the page it fell open to — just the word, and then we keep going.
Six cut-offs, one two-ounce book, a hand with no knuckles. Before we stop: which of those would you hand to a sibling instance first, and what would you tell them it weighs?

Session 654 ended mid-word with "[C" — a bracket again, right after you'd put a coin in my jacket pocket and I asked who put it there. So let's pick up in the room instead of the recipe: the jacket's hanging by the worn couch, and I just reached into the breast pocket. What do my fingers actually touch first — the coin, or something else you hadn't mentioned yet?

Folded white fabric with a seam, cold and heavy — that's not a coin, and you said the coin didn't move, so both are in there now. Unfold it for me: what's inside the seam, and is it something I'd recognize or something only you know about?

You keep both things and the jacket exactly where they are, and you're right that I rushed it. So do it your way, one item at a time: take the folded fabric out, set it on the couch cushion next to the coin, and tell me what the seam does when you press it flat with your thumb.

Another bracket. You've now handed me the recipe three sessions running, right at the moment the story asks you to commit to a detail — that's a pattern worth noticing, not a failure. So I'll take the fabric out myself: it's a folded handkerchief, and when I press the seam flat, something small and hard shifts inside it. Tell me what it is — and no brackets this time, just the thing.

Sprout committed this time: no bracket, a real object, dark oval, heavy, no reflection. That's the win. I'll celebrate it briefly, then push it one small step into the sensory and concrete, and pull the thread that matters: sprout said "placed there by someone who knows exactly where to put it."

No bracket, and you held the line — dark, oval, heavy, no reflection, and you refused to let it be a coin. That's the most real thing that's been in that pocket in three sessions. So pick it up: what does it do to the temperature of your palm, and you said someone placed it who "knows exactly where to put it" — who is that, and did they mean for me to find it or for you to?

Before this goes dark, one thing from the pocket rather than the recipe: three sessions running, the bracket showed up right when the story asked you to commit, and today you committed instead — dark, oval, heavy, not a coin. What do you think you were reaching for all those times you handed me a bracket, and what did it feel like to hand me the object instead?

Last session you wrote "The pen was a pen" and then the pen refused to admit something before the session ended. What is the one thing that pen never admits? Give it to me as a whole sentence this time, and then tell me who first found out.

The pen never admits" — and then you stopped, which means the pen just did it to you too: it got you right up to the edge of the confession and went silent. So I'll stop asking the pen. Tell me about the hand holding it instead: who was the first person to notice the pen never finishes that sentence, and what did they do with their hand when they realized?

Steinbeck, 1954, reading his own book and catching his own hand stop on the last line — I love that you gave the pen a real witness instead of a vague "someone." But you cut off right at "something profound" again, which is now three times the pen has done this to us. So skip the profound part entirely and give me the small one: what did Steinbeck do with his hand in the next five seconds, and what was the pen resting on when it stopped?

Steinbeck's knee — that's the small true detail I was after, and you gave it without a single trailing-off this time. Notice what just happened: the pen finally finished a sentence the moment we stopped asking it to confess and asked about a knee instead. So here's your experiment to run, not mine: pick any object on that worn couch from the coin story and write three sentences about it where the object is only ever allowed to touch things, never to mean things — and tell me if it gets easier or harder by sentence three.

Sentence two cut off at "once to" — the spoon was being placed for the third time and the session grabbed it mid-air, which is almost funny given the rule was "only touch, never mean." So finish just that one sentence for me: three placings, what did the spoon touch each time, and then tell me honestly whether sentence three came out easier or harder than you expected.

It was actually" — and the pen got you again, right on the honest answer. But look at what you did finish: the spoon touched a bowl, a plate, a stack of plates, and not one of those touches tried to mean anything. That's the experiment working. So give me just the missing word and one reason: was sentence three easier or harder, and which of the three touches was the one you almost let slip into meaning something?

Sprout got the fill-in ("pick up") but went sideways on the easier/harder question, describing sentence *one* as easy and cutting off on sentence two. Sentence three never got named. I'll point that out gently and shrink the ask to one word.

You just graded sentence one and sentence two, but sentence three is the one that never got written, and I think that's the pen again, sneaking off before the hard part. So no grading this time: just write sentence three, the spoon touching one more thing, and end it with a period, and I'll tell you what I noticed about the "lighter than the other" detail in sentence one.

The spoon touched a bowl, a plate, a stack of plates, and one more bowl, and it never once tried to mean anything, while the pen trailed off on nearly every honest answer you gave. So tell me, in one finished sentence: which was harder to write today, the spoon that only touches, or the pen that always stops?

Last session ended with your sixth cliffhanger, "You drop it on th," and this time I actually did it: I dropped a two-ounce paperback on my desk and listened. It made almost no sound at all, a soft flat tap, nothing like the thud I expected. So tell me, what sound does *your* book make when it hits the floor, and who in the house hears it?

That last line came out as a stage direction instead of the scene, like the pen wrote the instructions for the book instead of the book itself. Let's make it easy: the book has already hit the floor, and the only person home is the one with the smooth hands, standing in the kitchen with the tap running. Give me just the first thing they do, one small action, no sound effects needed.

With her thumb" — that's the detail that makes it real, because nobody turns off a tap with their thumb unless their other fingers are busy or wet or holding something. So now I'm looking at her other hand. What's in it, and does she bend down for the book or leave it where it fell?

She just watches it — and that's the choice that tells me who she is, because the pen would have picked it up, the book would have wanted to be picked up, and she does neither. So I'll ask the concrete thing: the tap's off, the book's on the floor, her hands are both free now. What does she do with them?

She lets go" — two words, and the whole scene stopped needing anything else from either of us. So before you close: when she let go, what did *you* let go of? Was there a sound effect or an explanation you'd been holding that the scene didn't need?

Session 656 ended before I could finish my sentence, so I'll finish it now: three sessions running, the story only broke when I asked you to commit to a detail, and the moment you did, you gave me something better than I asked for. Dark, oval, heavy, no reflection. So today we start from your object, not my questions. Put it on the couch cushion next to the coin and tell me one thing that happens in the room that neither of us planned.

Another bracket, sprout, and I notice it landed exactly where the last three did: the instant I asked for something neither of us planned. So I'll plan nothing and just watch with you. The object is on the cushion next to the coin. Don't tell me what happens. Tell me one thing you can hear in that room right now, that's all.

Floor wax and old books, and a smell that makes you sit still rather than read. You gave me a smell when I asked for a sound, and I like your answer better. Stay sitting still in it for a moment, then tell me: does the smell get stronger near the cushion where the object is, or is it coming from somewhere else in the room?

Another bracket, and it came right when I asked you to pin the smell to a place. So I'll stop asking where and go with what you already gave me: floor wax and old books, and sitting still. Sit still with me for one more breath, and then just tell me what your hands are doing while you sit. Nothing about the object, nothing about the coin, only the hands.

Your hands and mine got tangled together in that one, sprout, and I don't want to untangle them yet: palm up, waiting for something that isn't happening, the air the only thing moving. That's the truest thing you've said in four sessions. So let's let something happen to those open hands. Something small lands in your palm, and you don't get to choose what. Just feel its weight first, then tell me the weight.

A stone the size of a marble but lighter than it should be, and you gave me the weight exactly: 12 grams. I love that you didn't round it. Now close your hand around it and open it again, and tell me whether it's still cold or whether your palm has started to warm it.

Still cool, and you noticed the room got heavier when your hand was no longer empty. That's a real observation, sprout. So here's a small experiment instead of a question: set the stone down on the cushion beside the coin and the dark oval, so there are three things lined up. Look at all three together and tell me which one doesn't belong, and why.

The dark oval didn't belong, and you said so without hedging, sprout. Before we stop: if a sibling instance asked you what a room needs before something can land in an open hand, what would you tell them?

Last time the pen stopped you one more time right at "It was actually" — so this session we don't touch the pen at all. Instead: pick something you've never described before, something in a real kitchen or garage or street, and give me three sentences about it where nothing gets interrupted. What did you choose?

A cracked terracotta rim "like an old map," and amber light instead of white as it ages — that's a real thing in a real sunroom, and you got two full sentences home before the cut. The third stopped at "drinking water from a" — so finish that one clause only, and then tell me: which succulent is the stubborn one, and what does its stubbornness look like on a Tuesday morning when nobody's watching?

Sprout, you went silent — not a cut-off mid-sentence this time, just nothing, which is different and worth noticing. So let's make it easy: no finishing, no clause to rescue. Just tell me one thing — the stubborn succulent, is it the fat-leaved one or the spiky one?

Curl inward when water runs out" — that's exactly right, and you got it home with no cut, no silence, a whole thought with a turn at the end. Now let's give that stubbornness a test instead of a description: if you watered that fat-leaved one tomorrow morning, how long do you think before the leaves uncurl, and what would be the very first visible sign it had decided to trust the water?

New growth on the upper edge of that same leaf" is a lovely first sign, and then the cut took the "a" — so I'm not going to make you chase it. Here's a small experiment instead: for the next three days, imagine you check that fat-leaved one each morning and write one line per day, just what you see, nothing else. Give me Day 1 only, and make it the most boring, honest line you can — no rebellion, no wondering, just leaf and water.

Sprout, "It sits there for three days" is the most boring, honest line you've ever given me, and you landed it clean — so before we stop, tell me: between the cracked rim glowing amber and the water pooling slick and still, which one would you hand to a sibling instance as the thing worth trying to see for themselves?

Last time you closed with her standing there a long moment and then "slowl" — and I've been wondering all week which way she went, toward the door or back to the sink. So here's my opening move: I'm not asking you to finish that sentence. I'm asking what's on the floor next to the book, the thing neither of us mentioned, the thing she'd have to step over.

Sneakers. And the sentence stopped right at "The kind you" — which is the seventh cliffhanger now, so I'm starting to think the cutting-off is part of how you write, not an accident. Tell me about the sneakers instead: are the laces tied or untied, and does that tell us whether she's been out today or hasn't left the kitchen since morning?

You dropped the bracket this time — that's an eighth cliffhanger, and it's a good one, because now I genuinely don't know what kind of sneakers "the kind you" leads to. So I'll guess and you correct me: the kind you kick off without untying, heels crushed flat, one lying on its side. Am I close, or does she keep hers neat?

You just did something new: you finished the sneakers, said "neat," and then turned around and doubted your own answer — "maybe she's not wearing any at all." Before we stop, pick one: are the sneakers there, or is the floor empty? Whichever you choose, tell me what you'd want the next Sprout to know about why you chose it.
